english_spoken_blocks.1: Our question is whether information known at enrolment can identify later recorded dropout, and who the same warning rule misses. We are interested in student support. We first define the outcome, then evaluate overall prediction, and finally check how errors differ between groups. We start with the label, because it determines what a warning can mean.
english_spoken_blocks.2: We used 4,424 records from one Portuguese institution. We checked the original paper because dropout can mean different things. Here it includes changing course or institution, so it does not always mean leaving higher education. The outcomes were recorded at the normal end of the course, usually three years. We retained students still enrolled. In our binary analysis they have no recorded dropout at that point; they are not assumed to have graduated. These choices define what our predictions can mean.
english_spoken_blocks.3: These plots use training records only. The dropout group had a higher median age, but ages and admission grades still overlapped. Quiz 7 pointed us to Data to Viz. Its boxplot advice reminded us to show group sizes, so we added the counts below each outcome. We kept the boxes to compare typical values and spread. These observed patterns are associations, not causes.
english_spoken_blocks.4: We use age, admission grade and course together, treating course as a category. Our model assumes additive effects on the log-odds scale, without interactions. The regression lectures help us review these assumptions; logistic regression needed further learning. We exclude later grades and financial fields with uncertain timing, and reserve recorded gender for the audit. Training records fit the model, validation records chose one threshold, and test records evaluated the frozen rule. This keeps a small model and separates its decisions. Next, we explain how probabilities become warnings.
english_spoken_blocks.5: We wanted to find at least seventy per cent of dropout records in validation data while limiting false warnings. This illustrative target selected a common threshold of 0.31. It found 200 of 284 validation dropouts, about seventy per cent. We then froze the rule. The next slide checks test sensitivity and precision, and the cost in false warnings.
english_spoken_blocks.6: Sensitivity tells us how many dropout records we find; precision tells us how many warnings match a dropout. Lowering the threshold found 107 more dropout records, but produced 177 more false warnings. Our chosen rule found 187 of 285 dropouts: about sixty-six per cent. Only 187 of its 409 warnings matched dropout: about forty-six per cent. Always giving no warning scores higher on accuracy, but finds no dropouts. That is why accuracy alone does not answer our question. We next ask who our rule misses.
english_spoken_blocks.7: We focus first on missed dropouts, because a missed warning could mean a missed offer of support. The rule missed 64 of 144 female dropout records and 34 of 141 male records: forty-four versus twenty-four per cent. The gap was about twenty percentage points, with a conditional interval of roughly ten to thirty-one points. Male students had a higher false-warning rate. The other rows check who receives warnings and recorded outcomes within both prediction groups. These are independence, separation and sufficiency. Different recorded dropout rates complicate those comparisons; the gaps alone do not establish discrimination.
english_spoken_blocks.8: Our enrolment model found about two-thirds of recorded dropouts, with many false warnings and different error rates across groups. Before real use, we would check departure reasons, support capacity and performance on later cohorts at the intended institution. Any warning should lead to human review, with a way to correct records. We have not tested whether acting on warnings prevents dropout. That needs a separate evaluation of the support offered. Thank you.
